tip: This και isn't 'and': δεν έχω και πολλή εμπειρία (dhen ékho ke polí embiría) = I don't have that much – και adds a shrug to negatives.
One word carries the wish: μακάρι να μου τηλεφωνήσουν (makári na mu tilefonísun) = 'if only they'd phone me' – μακάρι να + verb is 'I wish/hope'.
'Careful not to' is πρόσεξε να μην (prósexe na min) – literally 'watch that not': να μην έχει ορθογραφικά λάθη (na min ékhi orthoghrafiká láthi) = that it has no spelling mistakes.
Languages wear the article: στα αγγλικά (sta angliká) = literally 'in the English'. Greek normally keeps the article here where English drops it.
No 'for' needed: περιμένω απάντηση (periméno apántisi) = literally 'I await answer' – περιμένω takes its object directly.
'What should I...?' is just τι να + verb: τι να βάλω; (ti na válo) = what should I wear? No word for 'should' appears.
Greek says 'show' where English says 'look': να μη δείχνεις αγχωμένος (na mi dhíkhnis ankhoménos) = literally 'not to show stressed'.
Κρατάω (kratáo = hold) also means 'last': η συνέντευξη κράτησε (i sinéndefxi krátise) = the interview 'held', meaning it lasted about half an hour.
Hiring is 'taking': δεν με πήραν (dhen me píran) = literally 'they didn't take me' – everyday Greek for not getting the job.
Greek folds 'are paid' into the ending: πληρώνονται (plirónonde) = they are paid – no separate word for 'are'.
You ask from someone: ζήτησα από το αφεντικό (zítisa apó to afendikó) = literally 'I asked from the boss' – ζητάω (zitáo) marks the person asked with από.
The idiom carries a dummy 'them': τα πάω καλά με (ta páo kalá me) = literally 'I go them well with' = get along with – the τα refers to nothing.
Being late is its own verb: αργώ (arghó). Here πάντα αργεί (pánda aryí) = literally 'he always lates' – no 'is' needed.
One verb English lacks: προλαβαίνω (prolavéno) = have time to, make it in time. So δεν προλαβαίνω να τελειώσω (dhen prolavéno na telióso) = I can't fit finishing in.
Receipts get 'cut': κόβω απόδειξη (kóvo apódhixi) = literally 'I cut a receipt' – the standard phrase for issuing one.
Λόγω (lógho) = 'because of', and the next word shifts to its of-form: λόγω της κρίσης (lógho tis krísis) = 'by reason of the crisis'.
Μένω (méno = stay) covers ending up in a state: έμεινα άνεργος (émina ánerghos) = literally 'I stayed unemployed' = I was left jobless.
A dummy-'them' idiom: τα βγάζω πέρα (ta vgházo péra) = literally 'I get them across' = I make ends meet.
Off-the-books work is 'black': μαύρη εργασία (mávri erghasía) = literally 'black work' – the everyday term for undeclared jobs.
Fear takes its own linker: φοβάμαι μήπως (fováme mípos) = literally 'I fear lest' – μήπως adds the 'what if' English handles with 'might'.
Contributions are 'stuck on' like stamps: κολλάνε ένσημα (koláne énsima) = literally 'they stick stamps' – from the days of paper pension booklets.
Retiring is 'coming out': θα βγω στη σύνταξη (tha vgho sti síndaxi) = literally 'I'll come out into the pension'.
Greek has no plain 'to open': you say 'I want that I open' – θέλω να ανοίξω (thélo na aníxo). English to-verbs normally become να plus a conjugated verb.
'In order to' is για να + verb: για να ανοίξω (ya na aníxo) = 'so that I open' – Greek has no plain 'to' form, so να does the work.
Greek commands mark duration: πάρε (páre) = take, one-off; περίμενε (perímene) = keep waiting, ongoing. A different verb form for once vs continuing.
Χρειάζεστε (khriázeste) is the plural 'you need' used for one person out of politeness, like French vous. Expect it from clerks and officials.
Greek's question mark is the semicolon: the final ; is what makes μπορώ να κλείσω (boró na klíso = can I close) a question, not a statement.
Clock times are plural: στις οκτώ (stis októ) – literally 'at the eights', short for 'at the eight hours'. Only one o'clock is singular: στη μία (sti mía).
You 'make' a card in Greek: να κάνω μια χρεωστική κάρτα (na káno mia khreostikí kárta). The same κάνω (káno) covers applications and licenses too.
Υπάλληλος (ipálilos) is one word for both genders – only the article shows who it is: η υπάλληλος (i ipálilos) is a woman, ο υπάλληλος a man.
